questions.q: Which business is in the secondary sector?
questions.why: Primary extracts raw materials, secondary manufactures, tertiary provides services.

questions.q: What does limited liability mean?
o: Owners can only lose what they invested
questions.why: Shareholders' personal assets are protected if the company fails.

questions.q: Which is a stakeholder of a school?
o: Students, parents, teachers and the local community
questions.why: Stakeholders are anyone with an interest in the organisation's activities.

questions.q: A bakery buys ingredients costing $1.20 for each cake and sells each cake for $4.00. What is the added value per cake?
questions.why: Added value = selling price − cost of bought-in materials = 4.00 − 1.20 = $2.80.

questions.q: A factory plans to expand, creating jobs but bringing more lorries and noise to the area. Which two stakeholder groups are most likely to have conflicting objectives?
questions.why: Workers gain more jobs and security, while local residents suffer the extra traffic and noise.

long.q: Explain two differences between a sole trader and a partnership.
scheme: B1: a sole trader is owned by one person; a partnership by 2 to 20 partners
B1: so a partnership can raise more capital / share skills and workload
B1: decisions: a sole trader decides alone; partners must agree (may disagree)
B1: profits shared between partners; a sole trader keeps all profit

long.q: A furniture maker sells a table for $350. The materials and other bought-in items for the table cost $140. Calculate the added value of the table and explain two ways the business could increase its added value.
scheme: M1: added value = selling price − cost of bought-in materials = 350 − 140
B1: one way, e.g. raise the price by creating a strong brand / better design or quality, so customers will pay more
B1: a second way, e.g. cut the cost of materials by finding cheaper suppliers or reducing waste, without lowering the price

long.q: Explain two reasons why many new small businesses fail in their first few years.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. poor cash flow / lack of finance
B1: explained, e.g. the owner cannot pay suppliers and wages on time even if sales are growing
B1: a second reason, e.g. lack of management experience / too much competition / poor market research
B1: explained, e.g. larger rivals with lower costs take customers, so sales are too low to cover costs

long.q: Explain two ways of measuring the size of a business, and why profit is not a good measure of size.
scheme: B1: one measure, e.g. number of employees
B1: explained, e.g. a limitation: some large businesses are capital-intensive and employ few workers
B1: a second measure, e.g. value of output / revenue / capital employed / market share
B1: explained with an example or limitation
B1: profit depends on efficiency and prices as well as size: a small business can be more profitable than a large one

long.q: A supermarket chain plans to open a large new store on the edge of a town. Identify two stakeholder groups and explain why their objectives might conflict over this plan.
scheme: B1: one stakeholder, e.g. shareholders / owners
B1: objective explained, e.g. want higher profits and dividends from the new store
B1: a second stakeholder, e.g. local residents / small local shops / the local community
B1: conflict explained, e.g. residents object to traffic, noise and the loss of green land, while small shops fear losing customers

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy, which need is at the top?
questions.why: Physiological, safety, social, esteem, then self-actualisation.

questions.q: A wide span of control means a manager…
questions.why: Wide spans suit flat structures with fewer layers.

questions.q: On-the-job training is…
o: learning while doing the job, often from an experienced worker
questions.why: It is cheap and relevant but may pass on bad habits.

questions.q: According to Herzberg, which of these is a motivator rather than a hygiene factor?
questions.why: Motivators come from the job itself, such as recognition; pay, conditions and security are hygiene factors that only prevent dissatisfaction.

questions.q: A manager makes every decision alone and tells workers exactly what to do, with no discussion. Which leadership style is this?
questions.why: An autocratic leader keeps all decision-making power and communication is one-way, from manager to workers.

long.q: Explain two methods of training new employees.
scheme: B1: induction training: introduces the business, its rules and the people
B1: explained, e.g. helps new workers settle in quickly and become productive
B1: on-the-job or off-the-job training
B1: explained with an advantage, e.g. on-the-job is cheap and practical

long.q: Explain the difference between dismissal and redundancy, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: dismissal is when a worker is made to leave because of their own conduct or performance
B1: example, e.g. repeated lateness or theft
B1: redundancy is when a job is no longer needed, through no fault of the worker
B1: example, e.g. a factory closes or a machine replaces the job

long.q: A hotel needs to appoint a new manager. Discuss whether it should recruit internally or externally.
scheme: B1: internal recruitment: an advantage, e.g. cheaper and quicker; the person already knows the hotel
B1: explained, e.g. less risk, as the hotel already knows the candidate's ability; motivates staff who see promotion chances
B1: external recruitment: an advantage, e.g. a wider choice of candidates
B1: explained, e.g. brings new ideas and experience from other hotels
B1: a drawback of either, e.g. internal leaves another vacancy to fill / may cause jealousy; external is costly and the person needs induction
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. external if the hotel needs new ideas or no current employee has the skills

long.q: Explain two barriers to effective communication in a business and how each could be reduced.
scheme: B1: one barrier, e.g. use of jargon / technical language the receiver does not understand
B1: reduced by, e.g. using simple, clear language suited to the receiver
B1: a second barrier, e.g. a long chain of command / wrong medium / noise / poor attitude of receiver
B1: reduced by, e.g. fewer levels of hierarchy / choosing a suitable medium and asking for feedback

long.q: A factory worker is paid $12 an hour for a basic week of 38 hours, with overtime at time-and-a-half. One week she works 44 hours. Calculate her pay for the week and explain one reason why the factory might pay a time rate rather than a piece rate.
scheme: M1: basic pay = 38 × 12 = $456
M1: overtime = 6 hours × 18 = $108
A1: total pay = $564
B1: reason, e.g. a piece rate may encourage workers to rush, so quality falls; or output is hard to measure per worker

questions.q: What are the 4 Ps of the marketing mix?
questions.why: These four elements are combined to meet customer needs.

questions.q: Primary market research is…
o: collecting new data first-hand, e.g. surveys
questions.why: Secondary research uses data that already exists.

questions.q: Penetration pricing means…
o: a low price at launch to gain market share
questions.why: Price skimming is the opposite: high at launch.

questions.q: Which statement about primary market research is accurate?
o: It is always more accurate than secondary research
It is collected first-hand for a specific purpose
It is cheaper than secondary research
It is taken from government statistics
questions.why: Examiners (2023): primary research was often wrongly stated as being more accurate; it is up to date and specific but costly.

questions.q: Sales of a chocolate bar have started to fall, so the company launches a new flavour in new packaging. What is this an example of?
questions.why: Changing the product to revive falling sales in the decline stage of the product life cycle is an extension strategy.

long.q: Explain two methods of primary market research a new café could use.
scheme: B1: questionnaires / surveys
B1: advantage in context, e.g. asks local people what food and prices they want
B1: a second method, e.g. observation / interviews / focus groups / test marketing
B1: advantage in context

long.q: A café raises the price of a cup of coffee from $2.50 to $3.00 and its weekly sales fall from 1200 to 1050 cups. Calculate the change in the café's weekly revenue from coffee and explain what this shows about the price elasticity of demand.
scheme: A1: revenue rises by $150
B1: demand is price inelastic: quantity fell by 12.5%, less than the 20% rise in price
B1: so customers are not very sensitive to price, e.g. they are loyal or there are few nearby rivals, and the price rise increases revenue

long.q: Sales of a company's soft drink have started to decline. Explain two extension strategies the company could use.
scheme: B1: one strategy, e.g. new flavours / sizes / packaging
B1: explained, e.g. renews interest among existing customers so sales rise again
B1: a second strategy, e.g. sell in new markets / to new segments / an advertising campaign / a price cut
B1: explained, e.g. reaches customers who have not bought the drink before

long.q: Explain two ways a manufacturer of sports shoes could segment its market.
scheme: B1: one way, e.g. by age
B1: explained in context, e.g. bright, fashionable designs for teenagers and comfortable walking shoes for older people
B1: a second way, e.g. by income / gender / lifestyle or activity (runners, footballers) / region
B1: explained in context, e.g. premium shoes for serious athletes at higher prices

long.q: A clothing company wants to start selling in another country. Discuss whether it should do this through a joint venture with a local business.
scheme: B1: an advantage, e.g. the local partner knows the market, customers' tastes, laws and culture
B1: explained, e.g. reduces the risk of costly mistakes and gives access to the partner's shops
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. profits must be shared / the partners may disagree
B1: explained, e.g. loss of control over how the brand is sold
B1: an alternative considered, e.g. exporting directly, selling online or using a local agent or franchise
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. a joint venture is best where the market is very different and local knowledge matters most

questions.q: Batch production means…
o: making a set of identical items, then switching to another
questions.why: Job, batch and flow are the three methods.

questions.q: Break-even output is where…
questions.why: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.

questions.q: Fixed costs are $2000; price $10; variable cost $6. What is break-even output?
questions.why: Contribution = 10 − 6 = $4; 2000 ÷ 4 = 500 units.

questions.q: What does an increase in labour productivity mean?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the weakest answers said output would increase rather than output per worker.

questions.q: A firm's break-even output is 4 000 units and it currently produces and sells 5 500 units. What is its margin of safety?
questions.why: Margin of safety = actual output − break-even output = 5 500 − 4 000 = 1 500 units.

long.q: A business has fixed costs of $18 000 a month. It sells its product for $25 and the variable cost is $13 a unit. Calculate the break-even output and the margin of safety when it sells 2000 units a month.
scheme: M1: contribution per unit = 25 − 13 = $12
A1: break-even = 18 000 ÷ 12 = 1500 units
M1: margin of safety = 2000 − 1500
A1: = 500 units

long.q: Discuss whether a car manufacturer should use just-in-time (JIT) inventory control.
scheme: B1: an advantage, e.g. less money tied up in inventory / lower storage costs
B1: explained, e.g. improves cash flow and frees factory space
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. production stops if a supplier delivers late
B1: explained, e.g. one missing part halts the whole assembly line, losing output and sales
B1: a condition, e.g. needs reliable local suppliers and good communication; no bulk-buying discounts
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. worthwhile if suppliers are reliable and close by

long.q: Explain the difference between quality control and quality assurance.
scheme: B1: quality control checks products at the end of production (or at stages) to find faults
B1: usually by inspectors, so faulty items are wasted or reworked
B1: quality assurance checks quality at every stage of production to prevent faults
B1: every employee is responsible for quality, so waste is lower

long.q: A factory made 12 000 units a month with 40 workers. After buying new machinery it makes 15 000 units a month with 30 workers. Calculate labour productivity before and after the change, and explain one possible disadvantage of the change.
scheme: M1: productivity = output ÷ number of workers
A1: before = 12 000 ÷ 40 = 300 units per worker
A1: after = 15 000 ÷ 30 = 500 units per worker
B1: disadvantage, e.g. the cost of the machinery / redundancy payments / lower morale among remaining workers

long.q: Explain two factors a supermarket chain should consider when choosing where to locate a new store.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. nearness to customers / population of the area
B1: explained, e.g. many households nearby means more customers and higher sales
B1: a second factor, e.g. cost of land or rent / parking and transport links / competitors nearby / planning permission
B1: explained, e.g. good roads and parking make it easy for customers to do a large weekly shop

questions.q: Which is a short-term source of finance?
questions.why: Overdrafts cover temporary cash shortages.

questions.q: A cash-flow forecast shows…
o: expected cash inflows and outflows over time
questions.why: It helps spot when cash will run short.

questions.q: The current ratio is…
questions.why: It measures liquidity: whether short-term debts can be paid.

questions.q: Which is a cause of a cash-flow problem, rather than a definition of one?
o: Customers are given too long to pay
The business is short of cash
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common error was to define a cash-flow problem instead of giving reasons it might happen.

questions.q: A business makes a profit of $15 000 on capital employed of $120 000. What is its return on capital employed (ROCE)?
questions.why: ROCE = profit ÷ capital employed × 100 = 15 000 ÷ 120 000 × 100 = 12.5%.

long.q: A business sells 2000 units at $15 each. Its fixed costs are $8000 and its variable cost is $6 a unit. Calculate its profit.
scheme: A1: profit = $10 000

long.q: A business's cash-flow forecast for March shows an opening balance of $2000, cash inflows of $15 000 and cash outflows of $18 500. Calculate the closing balance and explain two ways the business could improve its cash flow.
scheme: A1: closing balance = 2000 − 3500 = −$1500
B1: one way, e.g. arrange an overdraft / ask customers to pay sooner
B1: a second way, e.g. delay payments to suppliers / lease instead of buying equipment / reduce inventory

long.q: A sole trader needs $30 000 to obtain a new delivery van. Discuss whether a bank loan or leasing would be the better way to finance it.
scheme: B1: bank loan: an advantage, e.g. the van is owned once bought / repayments are spread over time
B1: a drawback, e.g. interest must be paid and security may be needed
B1: leasing: an advantage, e.g. no large sum needed at once, so cash flow is better
B1: a drawback, e.g. the van is never owned / total cost over time may be higher
B1: application to the sole trader, e.g. limited savings and a small business may find a loan hard to obtain
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. leasing if cash is short; a loan if the van will be used for many years

long.q: A business had revenue of $250 000, cost of sales of $140 000 and expenses of $70 000. Calculate its gross profit, its profit, its gross profit margin and its profit margin.
scheme: B1: gross profit margin = 110 000 ÷ 250 000 × 100 = 44%

long.q: Explain the difference between profit and cash, and why a profitable business can still run out of cash.
scheme: B1: profit is revenue minus costs over a period
B1: cash is the money the business actually holds, and cash flow is the money in and out
B1: a reason, e.g. sales are made on credit, so the profit is recorded before the cash is received
B1: a second reason, e.g. large purchases of inventory or equipment use cash but are not all counted as costs in that period

questions.q: During a recession, a luxury goods business is likely to see…
questions.why: Falling incomes cut spending on luxuries most.

questions.q: A multinational company is one that…
o: has factories or operations in more than one country
questions.why: Exporting alone doesn't make a business multinational.

questions.q: How might a rise in interest rates affect a business with a large bank loan?
o: Its loan repayments rise, reducing profit
questions.why: Consumers also spend less on goods bought on credit.

questions.q: A country's currency appreciates. What is the most likely effect on a business that exports most of its output?
o: Its products become cheaper abroad, so sales rise
Its products become more expensive abroad, so sales may fall
Its imported raw materials become more expensive
There is no effect on its sales
questions.why: Each unit of foreign currency buys less of the stronger home currency, so export prices rise abroad and demand may fall.

questions.q: Which government action is most likely to reduce unemployment during a recession?
questions.why: Lower income tax leaves consumers more to spend, raising demand, so firms need more workers.

long.q: A business in Country X exports machines priced at 50 000 X-dollars each. The exchange rate changes from 1 X-dollar = 2.00 Y-pesos to 1 X-dollar = 2.50 Y-pesos. Calculate the price of one machine in Y-pesos before and after the change, and explain the likely effect on the business's exports.
scheme: B1: the X-dollar has appreciated, so the machines are dearer for buyers in Country Y
B1: export sales are likely to fall, unless buyers value quality or the business cuts its X-dollar price

long.q: A multinational company plans to build a factory in a developing country. Explain two benefits and two drawbacks for that country.
scheme: B1: a benefit, e.g. new jobs, so incomes and spending rise
B1: a second benefit, e.g. more tax revenue / new skills and technology / more exports
B1: a drawback, e.g. local firms may be forced out by competition
B1: a second drawback, e.g. profits sent back to the home country / pollution and use of resources / jobs may be low-skilled

long.q: Explain how an increase in income tax could affect a business that sells luxury holidays.
scheme: B1: consumers have less disposable income
B1: luxury holidays are not necessities, so demand falls sharply (income elastic)
B1: revenue and profit fall
B1: the business may respond, e.g. cut prices, offer cheaper packages or reduce staff

long.q: Discuss whether a chemical manufacturer should spend money reducing the pollution it causes when the law does not require it to.
scheme: B1: a reason for, e.g. improves the business's reputation / image with customers
B1: explained, e.g. some customers prefer environmentally responsible firms, so sales may rise
B1: a reason against, e.g. higher costs reduce profit or force higher prices
B1: explained, e.g. rivals that do not spend may undercut it on price
B1: another factor, e.g. possible future laws or fines / pressure groups / effect on local residents and workers
B1: a supported judgement

long.q: Explain two ways that high inflation could affect a business.
scheme: B1: one effect, e.g. costs of materials and wages rise
B1: explained, e.g. profit falls unless prices can be raised by as much
B1: a second effect, e.g. demand falls if wages rise more slowly than prices / exports become less competitive / interest rates may rise
B1: explained with its effect on sales or costs
